name: Cagrilintide
lead: Cagrilintide is a long-acting analogue of amylin, a pancreatic hormone co-secreted with insulin that promotes satiety. Developed by Novo Nordisk, it is injected once weekly and is being tested for obesity and type 2 diabetes, both alone and in a fixed combination with semaglutide called CagriSema [1][10][12]. It is not approved as a standalone product in the sources reviewed.

A 2021 phase 2 trial examined dose-response effects of once-weekly cagrilintide on body weight in people with overweight or obesity [2]. Wikipedia reports that in the REDEFINE 1 study cagrilintide alone produced a mean body-weight reduction of 11.8 percent versus 2.3 percent for placebo after 68 weeks, and that 31.6 percent of participants lost at least 15 percent of body weight [1]. Phase 3 results of the combination with semaglutide were published in 2025 [3][4].

In appearance-oriented contexts cagrilintide is another systemic fat-loss agent in the clinical pipeline. The sources reviewed contain no forum or practitioner material on it, and the evidence is limited to company-sponsored trial publications and reviews.
infobox: Investigational; not approved as a single agent

paras: Cagrilintide has no approved indication. It is under study for weight management and type 2 diabetes alone and as CagriSema [1][5]. Registered studies include phase 3 comparisons of two versions of injectable cagrilintide with placebo in people with excess body weight and a phase 1 study of tolerability in people who did not tolerate GLP-1 drugs because of gastrointestinal effects [17][16].
Like other incretin-pathway drugs, cagrilintide reduces body weight systemically and has no known action on facial fat specifically. No published trial has studied it for appearance.

The phase 2 dose-finding trial tested cagrilintide against placebo and an active comparator in a multicentre, randomized, double-blind design [2]. A 2024 meta-analysis of three randomized trials (430 people) assessed cagrilintide alone and CagriSema; at 20 to 32 weeks, CagriSema produced greater percentage weight loss than comparators [5]. The REDEFINE 1 phase 3a trial (68 weeks, adults without diabetes) compared CagriSema, cagrilintide, semaglutide and placebo [3], and a companion phase 3 trial studied adults with overweight or obesity and type 2 diabetes [4]. A phase 2 trial examined co-administration with semaglutide 2.4 mg in type 2 diabetes [6]. Reviews describe second-generation weight drugs as achieving 15 to 25 percent loss, close to bariatric surgery [8].

Trial reports describe mainly gastrointestinal adverse effects, such as nausea and vomiting, that are dose-related [2][5]. A phase 1b trial assessed safety and tolerability of cagrilintide combined with semaglutide 2.4 mg [7]. Long-term safety is still being assessed and the sources reviewed describe no regulatory label. Products sold outside trials have unverified quality.

Cagrilintide activates amylin and calcitonin receptors, including amylin receptors in the brain, reducing appetite and food intake [11][9]. A 2025 study reports it lowers body weight through brain amylin receptors 1 and 3 [9]. Because the pathway differs from GLP-1, it is combined with semaglutide in the hope of additive effects [14].

Natural amylin readily forms amyloid fibrils, which complicates drug design, and the earlier analogue pramlintide needs frequent injections because of a short half-life. Cagrilintide is a stable, lipidated, long-acting analogue described in a 2021 medicinal-chemistry paper [10].

Other amylin-pathway agents are in development, such as eloralintide from Eli Lilly [15]. Reviews of the obesity drug pipeline place amylin analogues alongside GLP-1, GIP and glucagon-based drugs [13][14].

Human data comprise phase 1 pharmacology and combination studies, a phase 2 dose-finding trial, a phase 2 trial of cagrilintide with semaglutide in type 2 diabetes and phase 3 REDEFINE trials of CagriSema [7][2][6][3][4]. A meta-analysis pooled early randomized data [5]. No published trial has tested cagrilintide for facial appearance.
